demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Weapons or objects used as weapons

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

vignette:
Marisol Alvarez is a 43-year-old cybersecurity analyst who came to treatment as a widow carrying the aftermath of an event she still describes with a mixture of certainty and blankness: she knows she was the one who caused another person’s devastating injury, yet parts of the moment remain inaccessible to her no matter how hard she tries to force them back. The injury happened a little over a year ago during an argument outside a neighborhood gathering. What began as a confrontation escalated quickly, with raised voices, bodies moving too close, and a heavy object at hand that in another context would have seemed ordinary but in that instant became a weapon. Marisol remembers the sharp change in the other person’s face, the sense of things speeding up, and then the immediate realization that someone had been seriously hurt. Even in recounting it now, she does not offer a clean sequence. She stops, presses her fingers to her eyes, and says there is a stretch she cannot account for at all. She can tell you what came before and fragments of what came after, but the center of it feels torn out.

What remains most available to her is not a full picture but the force of what she feels when the event comes back. She is overtaken by grief so intense that it seems to arrive in her body before she has any words for it. At times she will be sitting at her workstation reviewing security alerts, and all at once she is hit with the same crushing sorrow, her chest tight, her throat burning, without any image attached. She knows it is about that night because of the emotional weight and because everything in her seems to drop into the same terrible recognition, but she cannot always summon a scene to go with it. That has left her frightened of her own mind. She has come to believe that if she cannot remember the missing pieces, then there may be something even worse she has done or failed to stop. At the same time, trying to remember feels dangerous, as though pressing on those gaps will unleash more than she can bear.

Her daily life as a cybersecurity analyst gives her fewer interpersonal demands than many workplaces, which has suited her since the injury. She spends much of the day behind multiple monitors, but even there she cannot fully control what she encounters. News alerts about shootings, online images of knives or guns, or even discussion of “weaponized” tools in digital threat briefings can jolt her. The visual presence of weapons or objects used as weapons has become especially potent. She reacts not as if she is merely reminded of something distressing, but as if she is pulled toward the edge of that night, back to the split second in which an object crossed from ordinary use into catastrophic harm. On days when a major violent incident dominates the news cycle, she has trouble staying with her work. She minimizes windows, leaves meetings early, or claims a headache rather than remain in front of images and commentary that leave her flooded and mute.

Confrontation has become difficult in a similarly immediate way. If colleagues begin arguing on a call, if a client grows sharp or accusatory, Marisol feels herself go rigid. What frightens her most is the speed with which ordinary conflict can change. She is certain now that heated exchanges are dangerous in ways other people underestimate. Because of that, she has made herself smaller over time. She avoids pushing back at work even when she disagrees, lets others take the lead in tense discussions, and has withdrawn from family situations where she expects disagreement. The consequence has been a narrowing of her life. Coworkers know her as competent but increasingly hard to read; relatives have told her she disappears from birthdays and holidays. She does not argue with them. She simply cannot tolerate the atmosphere when voices rise.

Trauma-related events are especially hard. Anniversaries, legal updates, or any public story that resembles her own leave her raw for days. On those occasions she becomes preoccupied with the injured person and with what was taken from them. The grief is not abstract; it is immediate and personal, and it sits alongside her widowhood in a way she finds difficult to explain, as if loss has become the organizing fact of her life. She sought help only recently after a workplace incident in which a routine conflict call escalated, someone on screen gestured angrily with a heavy desk object in hand, and Marisol had to leave abruptly, crying in the restroom without being able to explain why. She said she could no longer keep living at the mercy of moments that seem to come from nowhere. What she most fears is that the missing parts of her memory mean she is even more dangerous or unforgivable than she already believes. What she hopes for, cautiously, is not to erase what happened, but to be able to remember and live without being overtaken by grief each time the world shows her how quickly harm can happen.
